It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
  • I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub.
  • The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

And a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

The beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

It has been revealed that and Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

Sources indicate that the Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

Industry observers note that and perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

Industry observers note that as soon as Honda makes an electric scooter or motorcycle that could come close to replacing my Honda Silverwing, I am buying it. I need at least 80 miles of range at 50-55 mph. If it had a swappable battery I could carry with me, I'd be in Heaven. I think they have something like this in Asia, but not North America. Please.

In a recent development, honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

So here I am once again, Honda.

You’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

According to recent reports, just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

#152. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1600 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state.
  • Sources indicate that that’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial.
  • Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the organization notes the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

Sources indicate that that’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement demonstrates these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with crucial conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The new white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”.

Sources indicate that the solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

It has been revealed that osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

Sources indicate that the interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The company lists four concerns: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

Recent findings suggest that the pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:.

According to recent reports, this is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

Sources indicate that but this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release notes “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper indicates that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”.

According to recent reports, batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

Industry observers note that “Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

Industry observers note that that’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

According to recent reports, the “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS states high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

The business model is the bigger story.

Recent findings suggest that quantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and unveiled a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

In a recent development, there’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper notes the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD intends small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, said in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

Recent findings suggest that none of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

In a recent development, key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

In a recent development, also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

According to recent reports, but you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have noted so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

According to recent reports, so QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

It has been revealed that the question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production plans lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Industry News: Genesis reveals GV90 prices start at $100K+ in Korea, but it will cost more for coach doors

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000.
  • Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.
  • After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s upcoming eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis stated the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its upcoming extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a upcoming realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that indicates the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

Recent findings suggest that the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

It has been revealed that as a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

In a recent development, to power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis noted provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a newly introduced dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

And.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a latest standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

#150. Breaking: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (873 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Breaking: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • Recent findings suggest that both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and demonstrates,” according to Bloomberg.

Recent findings suggest that both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters claims the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and mentioned that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Industry observers note that also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

Sources indicate that so the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

It has been revealed that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

Sources indicate that it’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

In a recent development, toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

Industry observers note that after launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

In a recent development, starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, stated (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s latest EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a new vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

In a recent development, you can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante noted the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the new IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai declared its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the new IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai remarked the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Recent findings suggest that hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

On the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the latest Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Sources indicate that it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

Sources indicate that it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its fresh Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

Sources indicate that but the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

HMD took its first truck on November 2 and indicates it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler stated Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

In a recent development, the firm ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

It has been revealed that owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla launched volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla states its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how big that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

According to recent reports, the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that highlights whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a massive seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Sources indicate that our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

#146. Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1118 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first revealed it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.
  • On November 6, Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first revealed it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.

On November 6, Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

In a recent development, the reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of proposal, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

It has been revealed that and the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

Some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

Sources indicate that the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

It has been revealed that that’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t announced a single latest consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that introduced in 2017 and 2020.

In a recent development, tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

According to recent reports, even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

The pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car plans for Robotaxi in 2024. No new consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

According to recent reports, A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Industry observers note that tesla is becoming a company that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.
  • The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.
  • Sources indicate that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

Sources indicate that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a latest record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD noted the concern stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The firm noted it “immediately” debuted an investigation and corrected the concern so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit complications like this going forward.

BYD noted the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The tech giant said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD stated, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

Recent findings suggest that all versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

Industry observers note that in comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li stated the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

According to recent reports, the company’s bus sales were up 62.1% year over year in October, rising from 367 in October 2025 to 600 in October 2026. Overall, BYD’s commercial vehicle sales rose 68.3%, from 4,850 in October 2025 to 7,043 in October 2026. They rose 2.8% month over month, from 6,848 in September. BYD’s commercial vehicle sales total 55,489 units so far in 2026.

#143. Science For The People, Right On!

Science For The People, Right On!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today United for the Future launches at COP31 today with a plan to unite 100 million people in peaceful, non-partisan marches in cities worldwide.
  • Backers of the initiative include Christiana Figueres, former UN climate chief and a key architect of the Paris Agreement; Bill McKibben, author and co-founder of 350.org; Ram Ramanathan of Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego; and Sandrine Dixson-Declève, honorary president of the Club of Rome.
  • According to recent reports, together, they beckon citizens around the world: “Protect our future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today United for the Future launches at COP31 today with a plan to unite 100 million people in peaceful, non-partisan marches in cities worldwide. Their goal is to assemble the largest coordinated climate demonstration in history in order to put climate action back at the top of the political agenda.

Backers of the initiative include Christiana Figueres, former UN climate chief and a key architect of the Paris Agreement; Bill McKibben, author and co-founder of 350.org; Ram Ramanathan of Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego; and Sandrine Dixson-Declève, honorary president of the Club of Rome.

According to recent reports, together, they beckon citizens around the world: “Protect our future. Act on the science.” Their call asks governments to stop weakening climate protections and to deliver action that cuts emissions and protects nature in line with science.

Limiting temperature rise to a 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations, and one that’s often been politically contentious.

#141. The Netherlands Has €231 Million for Cleaner Inland Ships. It Still Needs Electric Freight Corridors.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (755 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

The Netherlands Has €231 Million for Cleaner Inland Ships. It Still Needs Electric Freight Corridors.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Netherlands is preparing to spend €231.2 million over four years helping inland ships replace fossil-fuel propulsion.
  • In a recent development, the newly introduced Dutch tender is considerably more sophisticated than a technology demonstration fund, yet it leaves an vital accounting boundary.
  • It has been revealed that the RVO programme can support battery-electric systems, some hybrid arrangements and other propulsion technologies, together with eligible charging and refueling facilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Netherlands is preparing to spend €231.2 million over four years helping inland ships replace fossil-fuel propulsion. The first €36.93 million tender opens on November 17, 2026, and battery-electric vessels are among the eligible investments. This is a serious step toward decarbonizing freight on the waterways that link Dutch ports and Europe's industrial heartland. But the programme's most important scoring calculation rewards emissions avoided per euro of propulsion subsidy while excluding separate subsidies for the shore infrastructure on which the ship may depend. That distinction matters when the commercial product is a complete freight service, not an electric vessel sitting beside a quay.

In a recent development, the newly introduced Dutch tender is considerably more sophisticated than a technology demonstration fund, yet it leaves an vital accounting boundary. My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment follows that boundary from subsidized vessels to working routes, drawing on my open, 98-page Inland Freight Electrification report.

It has been revealed that the RVO programme can support battery-electric systems, some hybrid arrangements and other propulsion technologies, together with eligible charging and refueling facilities. Its published explanation prioritizes electrification where practical. That is sensible: electric inland vessels are already operating in the Netherlands, and a subsidy should encourage the pathway that provides the required service at low emissions and acceptable cost.

The scheme also recognizes that a vessel does not operate in isolation. Applications receive points for commercial cooperation, cargo-owner agreements and the quality of supporting infrastructure arrangements. These are material criteria, not decorative promises. They are a welcome correction to programmes that fund novel equipment and assume the market, terminal and utility will somehow arrange everything else.

In a recent development, yet most of the available points are tied to projected emissions reductions per euro of propulsion support. That is a consistent measure for comparing applications for individual ships. It is not an accounting of the entire investment required to turn a diesel freight route into an electric one. One barge may need access to battery exchange at both ends of its journey, reserve battery inventory, grid capacity, a crane or handling system and a dependable service agreement. Some of those facilities can serve many vessels, making it hard to allocate their cost and value to any single propulsion application.

Zero Emission Services, or ZES, has already shown what putting the pieces together looks like. Its swappable battery containers allow inland vessels to obtain charged energy without each owner purchasing and maintaining every battery required by the route. At Moerdijk, a terminal arrangement combines battery exchange, handling equipment and access to an existing electricity connection. The ZES network is extending beyond isolated demonstrations, although operating sites, planned stations and funded vessel conversions must not be counted as the same thing.

Industry observers note that the difference between a capable ship and reliable freight is familiar to ports. Charged batteries must be available at the right time, terminals must handle exchanges without disrupting cargo work, and the energy-service provider needs enough committed traffic to finance its containers and chargers.

Recent findings suggest that the Netherlands deserves credit for recognizing these dependencies. It need not discard vessel-level grants or wait until every future route is planned before making early awards. But a second programme-level measure is needed alongside emissions per propulsion subsidy: what complete, repeatable electric freight service is each funded project helping create, and which shared assets make that service possible?

This matters all the more because the freight being carried will change. Fossil-linked cargo is likely to decline as coal and petroleum use falls, and ports should not size batteries, terminals and connections around the assumption that today's bulk flows continue indefinitely. A route with strong contracted demand may justify shared charging equipment while a low-utilization route requires a different architecture or timetable. The answer depends on the freight task, not merely on the specifications of an available vessel.

The Dutch programme is a promising way to accelerate the first investments. Its next achievement should be to show that those investments connect: cargo moving on named routes, vessels using dependable shared energy infrastructure, and operating data strong enough to finance the following corridor without perpetually reinventing the subsidy. The ship is the visible part of the transition. The corridor is what makes it commercially useful.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines the subsidy rules, the Moerdijk battery-exchange arrangement and the difference between vessel awards and operational corridors. The open, 98-page Inland Freight Electrification report contains the modelled cargo, fleet, battery-pool, terminal and investment evidence behind that analysis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

Recent findings suggest that the award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

In a recent development, the judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

According to recent reports, it’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, introduced in May, outperformed the newly introduced Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

According to recent reports, sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Industry observers note that global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a massive catch.

It has been revealed that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to upcoming data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

In a recent development, that puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of latest car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of newly introduced car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

Recent findings suggest that but here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

In a recent development, china sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Sources indicate that even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of latest energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

In a recent development, those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

It has been revealed that australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Recent findings suggest that as the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • So far in the renewable energy transition, silicon has shouldered much of the heavy lifting due to its excellent solar conversion properties.
  • In a recent development, there being no such thing as a free lunch, “raw” perovskite is challenged by natural conditions, namely, humidity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, perovskite is a relatively inexpensive material that has attracted thousands of researchers since 2009, when a team of scientists in Japan first demonstrated its use in solar cells. They achieved a solar energy conversion efficiency of little more than 3%, but since science loves a challenge, that was just the beginning of the story. In the latest chapter, the US firms Heliene and Caeulux have just introduced a new perovskite-enabled solar module that hits the jackpot at up to 27% efficiency, and it is already in commercial production, no less.

So far in the renewable energy transition, silicon has shouldered much of the heavy lifting due to its excellent solar conversion properties. Still, silicon is relatively expensive material that demands a complex manufacturing process. Perovskite is the reverse. Based on a naturally occurring mineral, synthetic perovskites can be lab-grown and applied to solar cell fabrication in a high volume, high throughput process similar to roll-to-roll manufacturing and other solution-based methods (see lots more perovskite background here).

In a recent development, there being no such thing as a free lunch, “raw” perovskite is challenged by natural conditions, namely, humidity. Tweaking the formula with other, more durable materials can resolve that problem. Researchers have also developed a tandem solution, in which a perovskite layer rests upon a silicon layer, providing an efficiency boost while minimizing the additional cost.

According to recent reports, in the US solar market, the sticky wicket is the current state of federal energy, trade, and tax polices. Still, the red-hot demand for solar energy in the US has motivated solar stakeholders to steamroll over those obstacles, attracting overseas investors (here’s one example) as well as upcoming domestic ventures.

On the domestic side, the Corning-backed manufacturer Heliene has been focusing on silicon while the startup Caelux has tackled the perovskite solar cell challenge with a glass substrate that can be layered onto other materials in a solar module. Now the two manufacturers have combined forces, with Caelux’s perovskite-doped glass boosting the conversion efficiency of Heliene’s N-type solar cells by up to 20%.

The Caelux-Heliene mashup comes at a time when Congress has finally put the wheels in motion to streamline the permitting process for energy projects. The two firms already have a running head start. On November 10, the two firms revealed that commercial-scale production has already begun on their Hybrid-Tandem™ solar module.

“Manufactured by Heliene in Minnesota, the perovskite plus silicon technology combines Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass with Heliene’s established silicon module platform to construct a solar module with two separate power generation layers that deliver higher power density,” Heliene explains.

“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” added Martin Pochtaruk, Heliene CEO and Founder, in a press statement.

“With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar,” Pochtaruk emphasized.

Stay tuned for the next development. The fresh modules are now in production at Heliene’s manufacturing facility Minnesota, with deliveries set for 2027. That’s just for starters. Caelux and Heliene have already targeted 29% efficiency and up for their next-generation modules.

The conversion efficiency improvement is the gift that keeps on giving. In the rooftop solar sector, for example, high-efficiency solar cells enable developers to squeeze more electricity out of a given space, making a rooftop array more economical for smaller properties that are otherwise shut out of the market. The cost of a smaller, more effcient array can also ripple downwards in the form of savings on labor, hardware, and transportation expenses.

According to recent reports, for rooftop solar in general, the boost in efficiency provides an opportunity to take full advantage of power sharing programs with local utilities, which enable solar owners to earn revenue and qualify for time-of-use discounts. The benefits can ripple into home energy storage systems and home EV charging as well.

On a larger scale, the space-saving angle can help alleviate land use conflicts that otherwise stymie solar development, particularly in the area of farm-to-solar conversion.

According to recent reports, although real estate development is by far the primary factor driving the loss of farmland in the US, solar opponents (looking at you, Brooke Rollins) have played the farm card to gin up resistance to solar development in rural communities. With efficiency improvements, the economic case improves for solar arrays on marginal lands and smaller parcels. That can be partcularly helpful in the community solar field, where solar arrays are typically smaller.

Sources indicate that additionally, the improved efficiency can help accelerate the uptake of agrivoltaic practices that balance energy-producing solar panels with grazing and croplands. These dual-use arrays can enable farmers to continue working their land while guaranteeing a revenue stream from the solar developer.

Furthermore, high-efficiency solar opens up new opportunities in the field of floating solar, where developers can make use of reservoirs and other human-engineered bodies of water instead of taking up space on land. By taking up less room on water for the same power generation capacity, floating solar can also squeeze into reservoirs where recreation and habitat conservation also compete for space.

Perovskite solar cells represent just one key breakthrough area in the US solar industry. Easing the federal energy permitting bottleneck is another. That can be a two-edged sword, enabling more fossil energy resources to flow through the pipeline. However, permitting reform could also prevent the fossil energy industry from running amok through federal energy policy.

According to recent reports, members of Congress are at the moment negotiating over the particulars of Senate Bill 5653, aka the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. If enacted as envisioned by the solar industry, the reforms will put a crimp in Trump’s “American Energy Dominance” policy, which has placed upcoming and burdensome restrictions on both wind and solar activity in the US while aggressively supporting fossil fuels and nuclear, alongside other renewables including biomass, geothermal, hydropower. Even energy storage has come in for a share of love from the Trump administration, further underscoring the remarkable exclusion of wind and solar from federal energy policy.

It has been revealed that the trade organization Solar Energy Industries Association, for one, is urging members on both sides of the aisle to ensure that permitting reform focuses on fairness, predictability, and certainty. In a letter to the House and Senate, SEIA emphasizes that solar and storage developers “cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid.”.

Sources indicate that “According to researchers at Wood Mackenzie, solar and storage represent 70% of the fresh capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026. Yet $120 billion in clean energy investment is caught up in current permitting delays, let alone the impact of permitting challenges to future deployment,” SEIA adds.

Sources indicate that of course, even if such a bill passes both Houses of Congress, US President Donald Trump could exercise his veto power, and he has already threatened to make copious use of it during his last two years in office. Nevertheless, US Presidents come and go, and this one is scheduled to go in January of 2029 — peacefully this time, one hopes.

  • Sources indicate that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company declared intends to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting new models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

Sources indicate that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company declared intends to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

It has been revealed that but don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t confirmed any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.
