💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.
  • It has been revealed that the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes.
  • Recent findings suggest that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

It has been revealed that the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Recent findings suggest that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Industry observers note that rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

According to recent reports, the lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

In a recent development, wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai states the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

It has been revealed that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Recent findings suggest that to start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Recent findings suggest that in case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the organization informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”.

Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”.

Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. “We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”.

#69. 5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1248 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change.
  • It has been revealed that however, these horsepower numbers come with a catch.
  • Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. The Impala SS (Super Sport) is a pure horsepower play that dates back to 1961, two years after the Bowtie brand released the Impala as a standalone model. Its numbers are still impressive, even by 21st-century standards. The retail version of the Impala SS from the 1960s, which covered two generations, produced up to 425 horsepower. The later Impala SS generations from the 1990s and 2000s were less brutish, offering between 240 and 303 hp, but they were still a step up from their more mundane counterparts.

It has been revealed that however, these horsepower numbers come with a catch. The output figures for 1960s Impala SS models reflected gross horsepower ratings, which generally didn't account for intake, exhaust, and accessory loads. When the 1970s rolled around, the auto industry was dealing with tighter emissions regulations and insurance companies that took a dim view of high-powered cars. By the 1972 model year, Detroit switched to net horsepower calculations to better reflect real-world engine configurations. Because gross horsepower ratings often varied from manufacturer to manufacturer, there's no standard way to convert horsepower ratings between the methods, but both still measure horsepower at the crankshaft, not the wheels.

Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net. Special race versions and modified cars are excluded. Here's how every Impala SS generation compares in maximum power output.

Recent findings suggest that the first Impala was a variant of the 1958 Bel Air, but the SS designation didn't arrive until the third-generation Impala in 1961. The second generation, without a Super Sport option, filled the two-year gap as the free-standing Impala model. The first Impala SS model's power output is a story of progression. The 1961 Impala SS arrived with a choice of V8 engines: 348-cubic-inch units rated at 305, 340, or 350 horsepower and a 409-cubic-inch V8 officially rated at 360 horsepower. In 1962, that king-of-the-hill powerplant could also be configured with dual four-barrel carburetors, increasing output to 409 horsepower.

Sources indicate that thanks to solid lifters, dual exhausts, and an 11:1 compression ratio, the 409's output rose to 425 gross horsepower for the 1963 model year. Chevy history buffs may also recall a 1963 Z11 lightweight drag-racing Impala with a 430-horsepower 427-cubic-inch V8. Keep in mind that this one wasn't a Super Sport model, nor was it a part of regular production, as only 57 were ever produced. The 1964 Impala SS continued with the same 409 from the previous year.

According to recent reports, horsepower for the second iteration of the Impala SS was in familiar territory, with peak outputs sitting at 425, but the Impala eventually took a different route to get there. To start, Chevy introduced an entirely new Impala with a sleeker exterior and a perimeter frame, ditching the X-type architecture of the outgoing model. The new looks helped the 1965 Impala become the best-selling single model of all time. A record 1,046,514 units were sold, with roughly 23% being SS variants. Impala SS examples from this generation still attract a lot of attention online.

The top engine for the non-SS 1965 Impala was the familiar Turbo-Fire 409-cubic-inch V8, making 400 horsepower. For the SS, Chevy also offered the L78 V8, a 396-cubic-inch V8 rated at 425 gross horsepower. A year later, the L72 427-cubic-inch V8 joined the options list, also rated for up to 425 hp. The powerplant featured a forged crankshaft and pistons, solid lifters, and a dual exhaust system. The SS 427 continued into 1967 and 1968, but with a slightly different L36 engine, still with 427 cubic inches, but now rated at 385 hp. In 1969, output increased to 390 hp.

Sources indicate that the final Impala SS came with 303 hp, which is the most of any modern generation. The supercharged V6 in the previous eighth-generation SS was replaced with a naturally aspirated 5.3-liter LS4 V8. That results in a zero-to-60 mph dash of 5.6 seconds, which is on par with a modern-day Mazda Miata – but remember, this was 20 years ago.

Sources indicate that that seems straightforward enough, but the final-generation Impala SS has some quirks that don't match its muscle-era badge. Notably, the ninth-generation Impala was front-wheel-drive, and naturally, so was the SS variant. Power traveled through a four-speed automatic transmission, albeit a heavy-duty version. Despite having an upgraded suspension that helped this SS go beyond a rental car-spec version, reviews of the day weren't particularly kind to the SS. In a 2006 road test, Car and Driver stated, "The SS seems to have been created to produce impressive numbers on paper with little regard to driver enjoyment." Nonetheless, the Impala SS's swan song continued through the 2009 model year.

After a quarter-century hiatus, Chevrolet resurrected the Impala SS for the 1994 model year. This time, it was packaged in a rear-wheel-drive sedan with a 260-horsepower 5.7-liter V8 engine under the hood. Engineers didn't have to dig too far into the parts bin. This LT1 V8 already saw duty in the Camaro and Corvette, although there are different LT1 versions over the years. However, the engine in the Impala SS was modified with cast-iron cylinder heads and a different camshaft. It was also tuned for more torque: 330 pound-feet in this application. By today's standards, a 0-to-60 mph dash of seven seconds is nothing exciting, but this was three decades ago, and this Impala SS weighed about 4,300 pounds.

According to recent reports, that bulk came from the full-sized Caprice, which underpinned this seventh-generation version. In effect, you could say that Chevrolet made a civilian version of the Caprice police car. The vehicle included an upgraded suspension, improved cooling, larger disc brakes, and a limited-slip differential. The five-spoke aluminum wheels and subtle strips of exterior chrome trim helped distinguish this Impala from its workhorse siblings. Leather upholstery was another clue. For its final production year, 1996, the column-mounted shifter was moved to the center console, and a tachometer was added. That's why low-mileage 1996 Impala SS examples still hold strong collector appeal.

Industry observers note that the short-lived eighth-generation Impala SS (2004–2005) stands out for a couple of reasons besides having the lowest engine output (240 horsepower). Namely, it's the only Impala SS with a V6 engine. Yet this is no ordinary six-cylinder powerplant; it's General Motors' 3.8-liter Series II engine with an Eaton supercharger, known for its broad torque band.

In a recent development, this Impala SS is based on the eighth-generation Impala, which was introduced for the 2000 model year as a front-wheel-drive sedan. Fast forward to 2004, and Chevrolet added the SS variant to the lineup, marking the first Impala SS that spins the front wheels. An upgraded four-speed automatic transmission controls the setup, but this Chevy also has larger anti-roll bars, modified springs, and Goodyear performance tires. As a result, 0-60 mph came in 6.5 seconds.

To go beyond a plain-Jane Impala, the automaker also added four round taillights (marketing language called this a Corvette-inspired treatment), black-only exterior paint, a small rear spoiler, leather upholstery, and a slathering of SS badges inside and out. This Impala was axed after 2005 to make way for the aforementioned 2006 Impala SS with a more powerful V8 engine.

Recent findings suggest that the Tesla Cybertruck was never as affordable as Elon Musk envisioned back in 2019, when the angular electric pickup truck was unveiled as a concept. Now, though, the American EV maker is selling a sub-$1,000 miniature version of the controversial model, right on the verge of its discontinuation.

The Tesla Cybertruck RC Racer was added to the company’s web shop today, as spotted by Tesla enthusiast Sawyer Merritt on X. The 1:10-scale remote-controlled EV features all-wheel drive, a rechargeable lithium-polymer battery, and independent suspension with plenty of travel.

The company claims its RC Racer’s 2.4-gigaherz radio system can maintain high-speed stability at distances of up to 326 feet (100 meters), while an optional Gyro feature adds counter-steering to help prevent spinouts.

Industry observers note that A single brushless motor sends power to both axles through a set of drive shafts, enabling a top speed of 37 miles per hour (60 kilometers per hour). That’s very impressive, and it makes the small-scale Cybertruck faster than all low-speed vehicles (LSVs) in the United States, which are capped at just 25 mph.

In a recent development, tesla bundles a USB-C charger in the box, which is a welcome addition in a world where smartphone makers are no longer including charging cables, let alone charging bricks. The Cybertruck RC Racer has an advertised run time of up to 20 minutes, and judging from the promotional video posted on the manufacturer’s website, it looks like a ton of fun.

It has been revealed that to charge the battery, the polycarbonate body needs to be removed from the chassis via the quick-release clips. Then, the battery needs to be disconnected from the motor and connected to the on-board charger, and charging can begin via the USB-C port on the side of the chassis. According to Tesla, a full charge may take up to three hours, which can be a bit of a buzzkill, but the manufacturer said it will soon start selling spare parts for the RC Racer, so buyers will probably be able to get a spare battery or two to keep the fun going for longer.

According to recent reports, the included transmitter has a side wheel for steering and a trigger for acceleration, braking, and reverse. Separate controls for the throttle trim, steering alignment trim, steering reverse, and gyro stability assist are also included. The transmitter is powered by four AA batteries, which are not included in the box.

Tesla’s Cybertryck RC Racer is available now for $350 on the manufacturer’s online shop, with the first shipments expected to arrive at customers’ doors starting next week. According to the company, the RC car is not suitable for children under 14 years old.

Study Pinpoints States with Steepest Warming Trends Since 1980

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.
  • Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, presently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius.
  • It has been revealed that to that end, a latest open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, presently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

It has been revealed that to that end, a latest open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” notes MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”.

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

By Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, MIT.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account unveiled the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

In a recent development, the order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print claims “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

In a recent development, the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and claims you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Industry observers note that tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

It has been revealed that and those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a massive reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

According to recent reports, I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

In a recent development, sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

It has been revealed that no point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

Sources indicate that and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

It has been revealed that if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla claims it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #65. Solid-State Cells Can Make The U.S. Competitive In Batteries Again: CEO

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1086 w)
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Insideevs

Solid-State Cells Can Make The U.S. Competitive In Batteries Again: CEO

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American companies may be playing catch-up to Asian giants in the battery business, but solid-state batteries could give the U.S.
  • Solid Power is part of a wave of young American battery startups—including California-based QuantumScape and Massachusetts-based Factorial—that are racing to commercialize solid-state batteries.
  • Battery scientists broadly believe that solid-state cells can unlock more driving range for EVs, faster charging speeds, and eliminate fire risks compared to current lithium-ion batteries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American companies may be playing catch-up to Asian giants in the battery business, but solid-state batteries could give the U.S. another shot at becoming competitive. That's according to the CEO of Colorado-based solid electrolyte specialist Solid Power.

Solid Power is part of a wave of young American battery startups—including California-based QuantumScape and Massachusetts-based Factorial—that are racing to commercialize solid-state batteries.

Battery scientists broadly believe that solid-state cells can unlock more driving range for EVs, faster charging speeds, and eliminate fire risks compared to current lithium-ion batteries.

Sources indicate that but the technology has proven extraordinarily difficult to manufacture at scale without defects. If you've been following this race, you'll know the technology has spent years being just around the corner.

Samsung SDI all-solid-state battery.

Solid Power, however, believes the wait will eventually be worth it. The tech giant expects solid-state batteries to reach select high-end EVs by the end of this decade, with broader adoption following in the early 2030s.

Sources indicate that it also secured a $50 million U.S. Department of Energy grant in 2024 under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law to support its development efforts.

Recent findings suggest that unlike some of its competitors, Solid Power isn't trying to build an entire battery. It specializes in one crucial ingredient: the electrolyte, which facilitates the movement of lithium ions between the electrodes.

Recent findings suggest that in a lithium-ion battery that electrolyte is usually a flammable liquid chemical. In solid-state batteries, companies are branching out into mainly three different varieties for the solid electrolytes: polymers, oxides, and sulfides.

Solid Power is betting on the third option. President and CEO John Van Scoter told InsideEVs in an interview that its flexible sulfide-based solid electrolyte design can help established battery makers incorporate the technology into their existing production processes and give the U.S. a way back in the battery business.

“All solid-state batteries can be the way that [the U.S.] can get back in and be competitive in the battery industry,” Van Scoter said.

The organization took a step toward that goal last month with the commissioning of its Mobius pilot production line at its plant in Thornton, Colorado. The goal? To manufacture and sell electrolytes from this plant to some of the biggest names in the automotive and battery industry.

Sources indicate that the firm has already been working with Ford, BMW, Samsung SDI, SK ON, and more names that are yet to be publicly confirmed. Rather than building complete batteries itself, Solid Power remarked battery makers can integrate its electrolyte into their own cell designs, test the results, and work together to refine the technology before production.

Sources indicate that van Scoter remarked the company has completed its joint development agreements with Ford and BMW. Its focus is now shifting toward working with major battery manufacturers to figure out how to scale production.

It has been revealed that the Mobius pilot line is expected to become operational by the end of the year, adding 45 metric tons of annual solid electrolyte production capacity. Combined with its existing facilities, that would bring the total pilot capacity to 75 metric tons a year.

In a recent development, so, what does all this translate to in terms of performance? When added to a silicone anode and a nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) cathode, Solid Power’s sulfide electrolyte can increase a cell’s energy density to 390 watt hours per kilogram and last over 1,000 cycles. (Modern NMC batteries with liquid electrolytes typically deliver around 250 to 280 Wh/kg.).

With a lithium metal anode, that energy density can increase to 440 Wh/kg, the company claimed, nearly double of an average lithium-ion battery today. However, these are just theoretical numbers. The final energy density will depend on the battery maker that builds the actual cell.

Sources indicate that “We create the magic that allows the cell to work,” Van Scoter said. “But it's up to the cell design as to energy densities, cycle life, all those other important attributes.”.

Another substantial advantage is that the organization believes its technology doesn’t need brand latest factories or expensive retooling.

“We can use standard [lithium-ion battery] roll to roll equipment in order to build all solid state cells,” Van Scoter mentioned.

Sources indicate that of course, solid-state batteries still have some familiar problems to solve. One is dendrite formation. These are the tiny, needle-like lithium structures that can grow inside a cell, potentially causing short circuits and capacity loss. Van Scoter said Solid Power had put a lot of engineering effort to solve that glitch.

The company isn't starting from scratch with automakers, either. BMW last year released images of a prototype i7 equipped with a solid-state battery featuring Solid Power's silicon anode solid-state battery.

BMW i7 Solid-State Battery Prototype.

BMW, Samsung SDI, and Solid Power have also entered a three-way agreement to develop the technology for commercialization. Samsung SDI will manufacture the cells, BMW will develop the battery modules and packs, and Solid Power will supply the solid electrolyte. The exact timeline of when we’ll see the fruits of this partnership remains unclear.

According to recent reports, other American solid-state startups are taking a more vertically integrated approach, developing the entire cells themselves. QuantumScape, for instance, is working with Volkswagen, Honda and other automakers to commercialize its technology. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis have already begun testing prototype vehicles equipped with Factorial's solid-state cells.

Solid Power, however, believes that the technology might mature first in defense applications, drones and humanoid robots.

“The qualification cycles are shorter and the cycle life of the platform is much faster,” Van Scoter said of drones and robots.

In a recent development, either way, U.S. automakers and battery companies didn’t quite capitalize on the lithium-ion battery boom, leaving that to Asian giants. Whether they can get solid-state batteries across the finish line first is something only time will tell.

#64. 12 Plug-In Hybrids With The Longest Electric-Only Range

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3041 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

12 Plug-In Hybrids With The Longest Electric-Only Range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in 2010, Chevrolet introduced the groundbreaking Volt — America's first plug-in hybrid production car.
  • Although it ultimately failed to attract enough buyers and was discontinued in 2019, the Chevrolet Volt was so far ahead of its time that many current PHEVs struggle to match its electric range.
  • According to recent reports, to compile this list, we evaluated the 2027 plug-in hybrids for the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in 2010, Chevrolet introduced the groundbreaking Volt — America's first plug-in hybrid production car. Packing a fairly major 16-kWh battery pack, the Volt had an EPA-estimated electric range of 35 miles, with later first-generation models rated at up to 38 miles. When the battery was depleted, it turned to a 1.4-liter four-cylinder engine with 84 horsepower to cover longer distances.

Although it ultimately failed to attract enough buyers and was discontinued in 2019, the Chevrolet Volt was so far ahead of its time that many current PHEVs struggle to match its electric range. In fact, out of the 12 plug-in hybrids with the longest electric-only range on sale right now, four have lower range figures. Of course, many modern PHEVs offer more EV range, with some models, like the 2027 Land Rover Range Rover Plug-in Hybrid, 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e 4MATIC, and 2027 Toyota RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid, capable of delivering 50 miles of driving without calling on the internal combustion engine.

According to recent reports, to compile this list, we evaluated the 2027 plug-in hybrids for the U.S. market, ranking them from the shortest to longest electric range based on EPA estimates. For models awaiting official 2027 figures, we used their 2026 EPA ratings, noting any powertrain changes. Excluded are models that are all-new for 2027 and not yet EPA-rated. Also, all listed prices include the destination charge. Let's dig in!

Sources indicate that the 2027 Kia Sportage is offered with three powertrains — a 2.5-liter gas engine with 187 hp, 1.6-liter turbo-four hybrid with 232 hp, and a plug-in variant with an electric motor for 268 hp combined. However, the PHEV's added potency doesn't translate into real-world performance, as it needs the same 6.9 seconds to reach 60 mph as the regular hybrid (per Car and Driver's testing procedure).

But this should surprise nobody, as the Sportage Plug-in Hybrid has a significantly larger and heavier 13.8-kWh battery, with the regular hybrid packing a small 1.5-kWh pack. As a result, it provides a meaningful EV-only range of 34 miles. The battery also supports Level 2 charging, so it can be fully recharged in only two hours. Once the battery is depleted, the Sportage Plug-in Hybrid doesn't turn into a gas guzzler and returns a respectable 36 mpg combined. Not bad, considering it also comes standard with AWD, unlike the gas and hybrid models, where AWD is optional.

According to recent reports, saving money on fuel by making the most of the PHEV's battery does require a few compromises, though. The Sportage Plug-in Hybrid starts at $42,085 in the X-Line trim, compared to $37,285 for the regular hybrid in the same trim. The hybrid Sportage is also available in lower-end trims, with the base LX costing $32,085.

The PHEV's larger battery also eats into cargo space. While the Sportage Hybrid has a major 39.5-cubic-foot trunk — only 0.1 cubic feet smaller than the gas model — the PHEV offers only 34.5 cubic feet of cargo capacity. Fortunately, there is no difference in passenger accommodation, with all Sportage models offering ample space for adults in both rows.

In a recent development, BMW facelifted the 7 Series for 2027, replacing the outgoing model's convoluted fascia with a cleaner front end that actually complements its monolithic, slab-sided proportions. As is customary nowadays, the cabin got a tech upgrade, with the 7 Series now packing BMW's Panoramic iDrive system with a parallelogram-like center screen, a thin panoramic display at the base of the windshield, and even a passenger screen. Meanwhile, passengers in the rear can now use the massive 31.3-inch theater-screen for Zoom video calls thanks to the built-in camera.

It has been revealed that BMW also massaged the 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 in the 740, which now produces 394 hp (previously 375 hp). The 750e xDrive PHEV variant remains largely unchanged, though, packing the same 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 hybrid with 483 hp and 516 lb-ft of torque sent to all four wheels. It's a potent powertrain, bringing the luxury sedan to 60 mph in 4.6 seconds and up to an electronically limited top speed of 155 mph, which drops to 87 mph on EV power alone.

It has been revealed that arriving next year, the 2027 750e xDrive hasn't yet received its official EPA figures. However, it should be rated close to the 2026 model's 35 miles, as they share the same powertrain. The 2026 750e xDrive is also rated at 24 mpg once the battery is depleted, for a total range of 460 miles. BMW hasn't unveiled pricing for the 2027 model yet, but expect a slight bump over the 2026 version's $111,550 starting price.

According to recent reports, the 2028 Volvo XC60 will offer more electric range than any other PHEV when it arrives in spring next year. Packing a large battery pack with a 37.9-kWh usable capacity, the heavily refreshed XC60 will cover 78 miles on electricity alone, more than enough for covering all daily driving errands, apart from the occasional long trip. In that case, the driver can always utilize the 2.0-liter turbo-four engine and expand the range to 590 miles.

Recent findings suggest that with such astonishing numbers, the refreshed XC60 makes you think twice about buying the current model. With a smaller 14.7-kWh (usable) pack, the 2027 Volvo XC60 Plug-in Hybrid has enough juice for an EPA-estimated range of 35 miles. That's still in line with current offerings in the PHEV space, but, damn, the 2028 model makes a massive case for itself with that EV-like range. Let's hope it doesn't cost much more than the 2027 XC60 PHEV's $67,595 starting price, because batteries are expensive.

The refreshed XC60 Plug-in Hybrid will also be more potent, producing 455 horsepower. The current model is no slouch, though. With 401 hp on tap, courtesy of an electrically assisted 2.0-liter turbo-four, the XC60 PHEV needs only 4.6 seconds to reach 60 mph. The PHEV powertrain is hooked to an eight-speed automatic and standard AWD. The XC60 offers decent interior room, though the PHEV's 21.1-cubic-foot cargo capacity is on the small side for the category. The cabin design is classically minimalist.

According to recent reports, lexus gave the NX a comprehensive mid-cycle overhaul for 2027, ditching the 2.4-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine in favor of an all-hybrid lineup. Crucially, the plug-in hybrid NX 450h+ comes with a next-gen powertrain with more power and an 8% larger battery. Lexus estimates a 45-mile range for the latest model, a significant jump from the 37-mile EPA-estimated range of the 2026 model.

Even if the EPA range turns out to be lower than Lexus' estimate, the 2027 NX 450h+ is worth the wait, with the first models arriving by the end of this year. For instance, while the ample interior space hasn't changed, there is a new, classier dashboard that comes standard with a 14.0-inch touchscreen and a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster. Lexus claims it also improved the driving dynamics, though in our first drive, we found that the Lexus NX doubles down on quiet luxury rather than chasing sportiness.

It has been revealed that that said, the 2027 NX 450h+ should be a bit quicker, packing 324 horsepower thanks to a more powerful front motor-generator. With 304 hp on tap, the 2026 NX 450h+ sprints to 60 mph in 6.0 seconds, with the 2027 model expected to drop a few tenths. Pricing for the 2027 NX is unknown at the moment, but it will almost certainly creep past the $59,505 starting figure of the 2026 model.

According to recent reports, in 2005, Lexus followed its parent manufacturer Toyota's lead by introducing the RX 400h — the world's first luxury hybrid vehicle. Since then, every generation of Lexus' luxury crossover has been available as a hybrid, with the current RX available with three distinct electrified powertrains: RX 350h, RX 450h+, and RX 500h.

The RX 450h+ is the first plug-in hybrid RX, combining a 2.5-liter gas engine with three electric motors for an output of 304 hp. As a result, the 2027 RX 450h+ sprints to 60 mph in 6.2 seconds. It also comes standard with AWD, enabled via an electric motor on the rear axle. With an 18.1-kWh battery onboard, the RX 450h+ has a solid EPA-estimated range of 38 miles. Thanks to Toyota's efficient series-parallel hybrid system, the plug-in RX sips fuel with a 35-mpg combined EPA rating once the battery is depleted.

The interior of the latest RX is luxurious and tech-forward, with an available 14.0-inch infotainment screen housing physical knobs and on-screen buttons for HVAC control. The cabin is more than spacious enough for adults in both seating rows, with a good 30-cubic-foot cargo volume — the same as on the RX 350h hybrid with the smaller battery. The RX 450h+ starts at $66,880 for the Premium trim, driving the price up considerably over the regular hybrid's $57,750 with the same equipment.

The fabled Mercedes-AMG E63 nameplate was discontinued in 2022, taking with it the 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8. But Mercedes-AMG didn't want to give up on the idea of a high-performance E-Class, so it used a novel plug-in hybrid powertrain in the latest E 53 Hybrid.

Recent findings suggest that combining a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 with 443 horsepower and a 161-hp synchronous electric motor, AMG's PHEV produces 577 hp as standard, or up to 604 hp with the Dynamic Plus Package and RACE START mode — 1 hp more than its V8 predecessor. The E 53 AMG Hybrid comes standard with AWD and a 9-speed automatic, reaching 60 mph in just 3.9 seconds.

It has been revealed that yes, this new high-performance E-Class won't sing V8 harmonics to your ears, but it has another trick up its sleeve: a big 28.6-kWh (21.2 kWh usable) ultra-lightweight high-performance battery. As a result, the E 53 AMG has an EPA-estimated EV range of up to 44 miles (2026 model), or 41 miles for the wagon.

Did we say a wagon? Yup, the E 53 AMG is also available in wagon form in the U.S., which should probably be the model you go for, as it has significantly more cargo space. Both models offer excellent cabin space, but due to the large battery, the sedan has a comically small 12.7-cubic-foot trunk. The wagon rectifies that with a much more usable 33.1-cubic-foot trunk, while delivering a 3.8-second 0 to 60 mph sprint with RACE START. The sedan E 53 AMG Hybrid starts at $92,550, while the wagon will set you back $96,650.

The hybrid pioneer has been significantly revamped for the current generation, transforming from the industry's ugly duckling to possibly the best-looking car on the market, with a sleek, coupe-like silhouette and athletic proportions.

Industry observers note that naturally, the Prius is a hybrid-only affair, available with a regular or plug-in hybrid powertrain. The former is an efficiency king, rated at up to 55 mpg combined by the EPA, while the latter provides an EPA-estimated electric range of up to 44 miles from a relatively small 13.6-kWh battery.

Because it's over 350 pounds heavier, the Prius PHEV is rated at a lower 51 mpg combined once the battery is depleted, which is still an impressive figure. The Prius PHEV is more powerful, though, producing 220 hp from its 2.0-liter hybrid powertrain. As a result, it accelerates to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, a solid figure for a family car. Unfortunately, while the regular hybrid is available with FWD and AWD, the Prius PHEV is FWD-only.

Recent findings suggest that due to the Prius PHEV's coupe-like shape, the rear bench is short on headroom, and knee room isn't particularly stellar, either. Still, the 20.3-cubic-foot trunk is decently sized for a compact family car. Also, while the 12.3-inch (8.0-inch standard) touchscreen houses most of the functions, the climate control buttons are physical.

Mercedes-Benz has thoroughly refreshed the S-Class for the 2027 model year, giving it a new design, advanced micro-LED headlights that provide better illumination without blinding other drivers, and of course, a new MBUX Superscreen infotainment with three separate screens and three built-in AI agents: Microsoft Bing Search, Google Cloud Automotive AI Agent, and ChatGPT-4o. Also, like in the latest 7 Series, rear passengers in the 2027 S-Class can now take video calls.

According to recent reports, what a time to be alive, right? Hey, at least Mercedes-Benz improved other parts of the S-Class, like the plug-in hybrid powertrain in the S 580e 4MATIC variant. The outgoing 2026 model combines a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 with a 161-horsepower electric motor and pumps out 502 hp. Thanks to its 22-kWh battery, it has an EPA-estimated range of 47 miles. The 2027 model keeps the same battery capacity, but bumps the output to 576 hp. So, while the range stays the same, the latest model will be quicker off the line. That extra performance pushes the price up to $136,150, compared to $131,750 for the outgoing car.

Unfortunately, the 2027 S 580e 4MATIC doesn't solve the biggest gripe of the 2026 model: the tight 8.1-cubic-foot cargo capacity. Mercedes-Benz lists the upcoming car's trunk at 9 cubic feet, which is simply too small for a high-end luxury sedan.

According to recent reports, want a PHEV with a long EV range and more cargo capacity? The Range Rover P550e Plug-in Hybrid can swallow much more cargo than the S 580e in its 40.7-cubic-foot trunk, while also offering an EPA-estimated range of 50 miles thanks to its sizeable 38.2-kWh (31.8-kWh usable) battery pack. With a base price of $131,350, it's also cheaper than the 2027 S-Class PHEV.

Sources indicate that naturally, the Range Rover PHEV provides ample space for adults in both rows, though you can't have it in long-wheelbase, three-row form. Not that you'll miss much, as the rearmost seats in three-row Range Rovers are only fit for kids. As you'd expect from a Range Rover, the cabin is laden with high-quality materials. But it won't flood you with massive screens, packing a 13.1-inch infotainment screen and a 12-inch digital instrument cluster on its clean, minimalist dashboard.

In a recent development, the Range Rover P550e offers more than enough performance for a luxury SUV. The powertrain centers on a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 and an eight-speed automatic, producing 543 horsepower after the electric boost. Land Rover says this is enough to move the 6,025-pound behemoth to 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and up to a top speed of 150 mph. The powertrain's efficiency isn't its forte, though, as it's only rated at 21 mpg combined once the battery is depleted.

It has been revealed that the smaller, sporty variant of the Range Rover Plug-in Hybrid comes in two flavors: P460e and P550e. Both are based on a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 engine and one electric motor, but differ in power output. The P460e is good for 454 horsepower and a 0 to 60 mph sprint of 5.3 seconds. Meanwhile, the P550e matches its larger sibling with 543 hp and drops the acceleration figure down to 4.7 seconds.

According to recent reports, both PHEVs share their larger sibling's battery pack, with 31.8 kWh of usable capacity, good for an EPA-estimated range of 53 miles. Still, they are significantly cheaper, with the P460e starting at $96,950, while the P550e is only available with the Battersea Edition trim, which includes goodies like a rear limited-slip differential and 22-inch forged wheels, and costs $113,850.

The Range Rover Sport has a similar interior design as the Range Rover, with an identical two-display approach and high-quality materials. Both rows offer ample space for passengers, though unlike the larger model, the Sport isn't available in three-row form with any powertrain. Since it's smaller, the Range Rover Sport has less cargo capacity: 31.9 cubic feet.

With a starting price of $64,150, the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e 4MATIC is more expensive than the 2026 Lexus NX 450h+ ($59,505), but it also houses a larger 24.8-kWh (23.3-kWh usable) battery pack that provides an EPA-estimated range of 54 miles. The GLC 350e also supports 60-kW DC fast charging, enough to take the battery from 10 to 80% in just 20 minutes. Still, Merc's hybrid powertrain can't compete with the efficiency of Toyota's hybrids, with the GLC 350e 4MATIC delivering 25 mpg once the battery is depleted.

Based on a 2.0-liter turbo-four, Merc's plug-in powertrain is more potent, too, producing 313 hp. Mercedes-Benz notes that's enough for a 0 to 60 mph time of 6.3 seconds, slightly slower than the NX's 6.0 seconds. The GLC 350e 4MATIC comes standard with AWD and a 9-speed automatic, which some buyers might prefer over the NX's e-CVT.

According to recent reports, inside, the Mercedes-Benz GLC pampers passengers with ample space in both rows and premium materials throughout. Its 22-cubic-foot trunk is also reasonably sized for a compact SUV with a fairly large battery. Unlike most modern Mercedes-Benz vehicles, the GLC 350e comes with a relatively small 11.9-inch infotainment screen in the middle, paired with a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster.

Sources indicate that the 2026 Toyota RAV4 arrived as an all-hybrid model ready to once again dominate its category. With a upcoming design and a powertrain lineup consisting of Toyota's fifth-gen hybrid and sixth-gen PHEV powertrains, the latest RAV4 bets on efficiency. A year later, Toyota further improved the RAV4 formula by equipping every PHEV trim with a NACS port and support for DC fast charging.

According to recent reports, the powertrain itself remained largely unchanged, though. Based around a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine and three electric motors (AWD), it produced 324 hp in 2026 form, enough for a 0 to 60 mph time of just 5.4 seconds. That's quick for a compact crossover, with Toyota even launching the fun-to-drive RAV4 GR Sport variant around this powertrain. As per Toyota's estimates, the entry-level 2027 RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid SE has a range of 52 miles. Still, the 2026 model is rated at an EPA-estimated 54 miles, although Toyota initially estimated a shorter 52-mile range.

According to recent reports, the latest RAV4 can comfortably accommodate adults in both rows, while boasting a 33.5-cubic-foot trunk. #62. Tech Report: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1012 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tech Report: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely latest, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the manufacturer’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

In a recent development, the ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

In a recent development, if I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Sources indicate that plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be rapidly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

According to recent reports, it may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

According to recent reports, and that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as swiftly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

According to recent reports, I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road promptly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

Industry observers note that for years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions rapidly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally).

OpenAI, the manufacturer behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

It has been revealed that one might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the manufacturer’s revenue was actually up by 50%! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

It has been revealed that openAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

In a recent development, frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?

In a recent development, as we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?

Recent findings suggest that the one substantial player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

Industry observers note that “The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings. In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble.”.

Why can’t the leaders of these companies just ask their chatbots how to turn a profit and implement their answers? Well, one of the answers might have been regulatory capture and blocking others from entering the market, but that dream may now be out the window. In my humble opinion, 2027 could be a very interesting year for AI companies, and that might involve a major popping noise.

Back in 2015, Toyota teased us with the perfect car: The S-FR concept, a Miata-fighting two-door roadster set to be a little sibling to what was then the Scion FR-S. After that big reveal, the little car just vanished into thin air, never to be seen again except in my most beautiful and hopeful dreams. Now, though, it seems those winds could be changing once again. A new report out of Japan says that Toyota is thinking about finally bringing the S-FR to production.

Industry observers note that the news comes from Japanese outlet Response, which mentioned the S-FR could finally hit dealerships as early as 2027, though not quite as it was originally designed. Instead of being a Miata fighter, the new S-FR would be even smaller, built on the platform of a third-generation Daihatsu Copen. Daihatsu teased a new Copen with its K-Open concept last year (pictured below), and it wouldn't be hard for Toyota to throw a bit of design work at its subsidiary's kei car and bring a proper S-FR to market.

Recent findings suggest that of course, a modern kei car would be a pretty substantial rework of the S-FR formula. Previous Copens have all been front-wheel drive, so shifting to a rear-wheel-drive platform to accommodate an S-FR twin would make it more of a sports car, too. The original concept was neither modern nor kei, with a 1.5-liter naturally-aspirated four-cylinder engine and a rear seat, the former of which would be impossible and the latter unlikely in a kei car. In fact, the whole design would need to shrink to meet kei car requirements, making it even less likely we'd get a version here in the States. Still, Toyota is already bringing us one kei, so maybe we can dream.

It has been revealed that even if it's only for the Japanese market, I hope this report from Response is accurate and that Toyota is really thinking about bringing the S-FR to market as a Copen variant. It just makes sense — take your beloved-but-abandoned little sports car concept and apply it to your soon-to-be-resurrected little sports car platform. Maybe, if we're really lucky, Toyota will bring some over to the States as the same sort of low-speed vehicle as the KEI-01. I'd happily tune a limiter out of one of these just to get to drive it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that BYD has already shown that charging an EV doesn’t have to take much longer than filling a gas tank. Now it’s tackling another problem: getting enough electricity to a fast charger in the first place.

It has been revealed that its latest site in the Abu Dhabi desert combines solar panels, battery storage, Flash Charging, and a robotic arm that plugs in the car. BYD states the system can work independently of the electricity grid, potentially bringing fast charging to places where a power connection may not be feasible. The proposition is pretty simple: Solar panels generate electricity, batteries store it, and the charger sends it to an EV.

Industry observers note that battery-backed charging is becoming more common because it lets stations deliver more power than their grid connection alone can supply, while also reducing demand on the grid during busy periods. Tesla’s biggest Supercharger site, which it opened earlier this year, also uses solar panels and Tesla's Megapack batteries. Companies like Electric Era and Beam Global specialize in battery-backed charging. Even BYD Flash chargers not located in the middle of the desert and not supplied by solar panels use on-site energy storage to boost power delivery.

Recent findings suggest that each of BYD's T-shaped Flash chargers is hooked up to two 185-kilowatt-hour storage batteries, for 370 kWh total. These draw power from the grid at around 100 to 560 kilowatts, then supply the car at a much higher rate. The chargers can send up to 1,500 kW through one cable, or up to 1,000 kW when both are in use at the same time.

Industry observers note that adding solar panels into the equation means some or even all of that electricity can be generated on-site. However, BYD hasn’t disclosed the battery capacity or solar output of this upcoming desert installation. So it's not clear how many cars the station can charge—or how swiftly—on solar power alone.

The charging hardware is impressively quick. With BYD’s latest 1,500-kW Flash chargers, compatible cars running its second-generation Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or hit 97% in nine minutes.

Now that infrastructure is going global. The company states it plans to establish 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, but it hasn’t specified how many will offer solar power, off-grid operation, or that robotic arm.

Europe is getting a taste of BYD’s Flash charging with sites up and running in Italy, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom. Canada is coming soon too. The only vehicle it currently sells in Europe that can fully utilize its power is the Denza Z9 GT. During a demonstration, the electric wagon charged from 10% to 80% in six minutes and 32 seconds, reaching 97% in nine minutes and 22 seconds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that people are capable of doing some supremely stupid things in cars.
  • According to recent reports, close calls happen more often than you might expect, especially when we live in an era where vehicles are equipped with every warning along with literal bells and whistles to tell drivers they might hit something.
  • In a recent development, years ago, while in the city for the New York International Auto Show, I was lucky enough to be driving a well-equipped 2021 Maserati Levante GTS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that people are capable of doing some supremely stupid things in cars. We've seen the warnings from informational videos over the decades, and our personal blunders and experiences have demonstrated this point, too. We can, of course, be attentive behind the wheel, but that doesn't account for the others who aren't while on the road. It's partly why dash cams and their resulting videos have gained so much traction in recent years. While someone's dumb decision may end up in disaster, others might end in close calls — moments where destruction was inches away.

According to recent reports, close calls happen more often than you might expect, especially when we live in an era where vehicles are equipped with every warning along with literal bells and whistles to tell drivers they might hit something. This week, we don't want to know about the little near-misses — we want to know about the substantial ones that haunt you. Tell us about the misses that had they been hits, would've made for calamity.

In a recent development, years ago, while in the city for the New York International Auto Show, I was lucky enough to be driving a well-equipped 2021 Maserati Levante GTS. I had taken it on a scenic drive along the Belt Parkway to Amityville, and on my return to Brooklyn, I hit a bit of traffic. About 10 minutes into my drive, in a 35 mph residential zone, an Audi Q5 came speeding up behind me. I reactively slowed down to let it fly past.

I watched as this Q5 blazed through a red light and hit another car, a fairly latest Subaru, before the Q5 went spinning into the other side of the intersection. That was near miss number one. Two people got out of the smashed Q5 and bolted. Instinctively, I wanted to stop and help, but I was in a part of New York I was unfamiliar with in a six-figure vehicle that wasn't mine. Instead, I opted to get around the scene.

According to recent reports, seconds later, a Ford Taurus came up on my bumper, then rapidly maneuvered ahead to cut me off before making a turn into a parking lot where it then stopped, and a cop hopped out and proceeded to stop a kid who had run from the crash scene. The Taurus was never put in park, though, and it started rolling towards the Maserati. I panicked, trying to figure out how to reverse it with its weird shifter.

Industry observers note that the cop saw what was happening and was able to catch the car about an inch away from the Maserati. Near miss number two. Meanwhile, another cop had arrested the kid. After a deep breath and a phone call to my husband, still quite shaken, I made my way back to Brooklyn.

Sources indicate that it might not have been the greatest near-miss, but the feelings I had nearly five years ago remain strong to this day. With that chaos in mind, what was your most unforgettable close call? Tell us all about it and why it holds critical space in your memory bank in the comments below.

Tech Report: Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested.
  • And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
  • The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the manufacturer started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the manufacturer started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

Industry observers note that that personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Industry observers note that then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk stated the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

In a recent development, tesla’s answer to all those owners is a fresh car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if consumers join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

Industry observers note that and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it.
